publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. source_text: THESIS I. JACOBUS Arminius, & qui ejus dogmata in Belgio secuti Remonstrantes dicuntur, quemadmodum in explicanda libertatis humanae natura, cum Molina & ejus discipulis consentiunt; ita quoque videntur eam eodem modo cum Providentiae Divinae decretis conciliare. Saltem huc tendunt quae docet Arminius Responsione ad Articulum 7. Operum ipsius pagina 143. Ubi non negat quidem Deum Decreto suo aeterno futura contingentia praedefinivisse & praedeterminasse; sed distinguit duplicem Dei determinationem qua statuit ut aliquid fiat: Unam talem, qua, posita qualicunque actione, motione, impulsu Dei, causa secunda libera manet quoad potentiam & usum potentiae, ad agendum, vel non agendum, adeo ut actionem suam, si velit, suspendere possit. alteram talem, qua posita non manet libera causa secunda, saltem non ad usum potentiae, ut actionem suam suspendere possit, posita actione, motione, & impulsu Dei; sed ex qua fit ut necessario in alteram partem flectatur, ablata indifferentia ad alterutram partem; antequam actus ipse determinatus productus sit a creatura libera. Si priore modo vox determinationis intelligatur, talem determinationem Dei non negat respectu futurorum liberorum & contingentium. Sed si secundo sensu sumatur vox determinationis, plane negat Deum futura contingentia decreto suo determinasse ad alterutram partem.
english: James Arminius, and those in the Low Countries who followed his teachings and are called Remonstrants, agree with Molina and his disciples in explaining the nature of human freedom. They also seem to reconcile that freedom with the decrees of God's providence in the same way. Arminius's teaching in his Response to Article 7, Works page 143, at least points that way.

There he does not deny that God by his eternal decree predefined and predetermined future contingents. But he distinguishes two kinds of divine determination by which God settles that something shall happen. In the first, whatever action, motion or impulse of God is in place, the free second cause remains free both in its power and in the use of that power to act or not act, so that it can suspend its action if it wishes.

In the second, once God's action, motion and impulse are in place, the second cause does not remain free, at least not in the use of its power so as to be able to suspend its action. Instead it is necessarily bent to one side, its indifference to either side being removed, before the determined act is produced by the free creature.

If 'determination' is taken in the first sense, he does not deny that God so determines future free and contingent things. If it is taken in the second sense, he flatly denies that God by his decree determined future contingents to one side or the other.

source_text: II. Porro distincte non explicat quomodo ista simul constent, ut actio quaedam aeterno Dei decreto determinata sit, & tamen posita illa determinatione voluntas semper maneat indifferens ad talem actionem, & possit semper illam elicere, vel non elicere. Ex iis tamen quae subjungit colligendum relinquit rem ita se habere, quoniam Deus ut sua decreta circa hominum actus exequatur, non aliter movet eorum voluntatem quam iis administrando & proponendo ea objecta atque argumenta, quibus ad volendum quidem inducantur, sed ita tamen ut semper in eorum potestate sit objectis illis non moveri. Verum illius Discipuli, ut inter alios Nicolaus Grevinchovius, ad nodum hunc solvendum diserte adhibent scientiam mediam, sicuti solent Jesuitae plurimi, qua ratione thesibus praecedentibus expositum fuit.
english: He does not clearly explain how these two things fit together: that an action is determined by God's eternal decree, and yet, with that determination in place, the will always remains indifferent to the action and always able to produce it or not.

From what he adds, however, he leaves us to infer that it works like this. To carry out his decrees about human acts, God moves men's wills only by supplying and setting before them objects and arguments that do induce them to will, yet in such a way that it always remains in their power not to be moved by those objects.
His disciples, such as Nicolaus Grevinchoven among others, expressly bring in middle knowledge to untie this knot, as most Jesuits do, in the way set out in the preceding theses.

source_text: III. Sed inter eos etiam Reformatos qui alioqui videntur ab Arminiano dogmate alieni, & Dordracenae Synodo subscribunt, reperiuntur nonnulli qui hanc quoque viam sequuntur, ut Providentiae Divinae decreta cum arbitrii humani libertate concilient. Quo de numero est Robertus Baronius Abredoniae in Scotia ante aliquot annos Theologiae Professor. Is enim in Metaphysica ad Theologiae usum accommodata Fonsecae doctrinam hac in parte laudat, eique aperte subscribit. Sect. 12. disput. 2. num. 65.
english: Yet even among the Reformed who otherwise seem far from the Arminian teaching and subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some follow this same way of reconciling the decrees of God's providence with the freedom of human choice.

One of them is Robert Baron, some years ago professor of theology at Aberdeen in Scotland. In his Metaphysics adapted to the use of theology he praises Fonseca's teaching on this point and openly endorses it: section 12, disputation 2, number 65.

source_text: IV. Nam eo in loco proponit duas conclusiones Fonsecae quas dicit sibi maxime utiles videri ad stabiliendam concordiam Providentiae Divinae, & libertatis arbitrii humani. Prior est quod ante omnem praescientiam actuum liberorum eorum nullus fuit ab aeterno praedefinitus. Quorum verborum, inquit, hic sensus est, Antequam Deus praescivit, vel praevidit in quam partem humanae voluntates inclinaturae essent, si hae vel illae occasiones iis offerrentur, non absolute voluit voluntatem elicere has actiones potius quam illas, neque decrevit concurrere ad eliciendas has actiones potius quam illas. Secunda conclusio est, Postquam Deus secundum nostrum concipiendi modum praevidit in quam partem inclinaturae essent nostrae voluntates, cum hae aut illae occasiones iis offerrentur, ab aeterno decrevit cum voluntatibus nostris concurrere ad eliciendas, in hoc vel illo tempore, has vel illas actiones, in quas voluntates inclinaturas praevidebat. Exempli causa, Deus ab aeterno praevidit Adamum, si tentaretur ab Uxore, appetiturum pomum, & propterea decrevit concurrere cum Adamo ad eliciendam appetitionem pomi.
english: Baron there cites two conclusions of Fonseca which, by his own account, strike him as especially helpful for showing that God's providence and the freedom of human choice agree. First: none of our free acts was predefined from eternity prior to every foreknowledge of them.

He glosses this as follows. Until God had foreknown or foreseen in which direction human wills would turn, were this or that occasion put to them, he neither willed absolutely that the will should elicit one set of actions over another, nor decreed to concur in eliciting one set rather than another.

Second: once God, as we must conceive it, had foreseen the direction our wills would take when given this or that occasion, he decreed from eternity to concur with them at the relevant times in eliciting precisely the actions he saw they would turn toward.
Thus, to take an example, God foresaw from eternity that Adam, if tempted by his wife, would desire the fruit, and for that reason decreed to concur with Adam in eliciting that desire.

source_text: V. Sic ergo explicari posse putat ordinem Decreti Divini circa primum illud peccatum. Primo, inquit, Deus habet praescientiam conditionatam qua praevidet Adamum appetiturum pomum si offeratur illi talis occasio; habet item praescientiam, qua novit se posse illam actionem Adami dirigere ad gloriam suam. Secundo, quia praevidit se posse ex illa prava actione Adami, quam Adamus habiturus esset, si ei offeratur talis occasio; quia, inquam, praevidit se posse ex illa actione magnum bonum elicere, scilicet, manifestationem gloriae suae, ideo voluit illam occasionem Adamo offerri, id est, voluit permittere Evam a Serpente seductam Adamum tentare. Tertio, secundum praescientiam non conditionatam, sed absolutam praevidit voluntatem Adami inclinaturam esse ad appetitionem pomi, eo scilicet tempore quo Adamus tentandus esset. Quarto, partim ne praeriperet Adamo usum sui liberi Arbitrii, partim ut gloriam suam manifestaret, decrevit concurrere cum voluntate Adami ad eliciendam illam volitionem. Unde evidenter patet non ideo Adamum fuisse lapsurum, vel appetiturum pomum, quia Deus decrevit cum ejus voluntate concurrere ad eliciendam appetitionem; sed contra, ideo Deum decrevisse concurrere ad eliciendam illam actionem potius quam aliam, quia praevidit voluntatem ejus in talem partem inclinaturam fuisse, cum talis occasio illi offerretur.
english: So he thinks the order of God's decree about that first sin can be explained as follows. 'First,' he says, 'God has a conditional foreknowledge by which he foresees that Adam will desire the fruit if such an occasion is offered him. He also has a foreknowledge by which he knew that he could direct that act of Adam to his own glory.

Second, he foresaw that from the wicked act Adam would perform if such an occasion were offered him, he could bring a great good, namely the display of his glory. Because of this, I say, he willed that the occasion be offered to Adam; that is, he willed to permit Eve, deceived by the serpent, to tempt Adam.
Third, by a foreknowledge that is not conditional but absolute, he foresaw that Adam's will would lean toward desiring the fruit at the time when Adam was to be tempted.
Fourth, partly so as not to take from Adam the use of his free choice, and partly to display his glory, he decreed to concur with Adam's will in producing that volition.

From this it plainly follows that Adam was not going to fall, or to desire the fruit, because God decreed to concur with his will in producing the desire. On the contrary, God decreed to concur in producing that action rather than another because he foresaw that Adam's will would lean that way when such an occasion was offered him.'

source_text: VI. Ex quibus postea dicit manifeste sequi Deum per decreta Providentiae suae non imponere nobis necessitatem hoc vel illud volendi: ac praeterea Dei decreta non esse causas cur hoc vel illo tempore, hanc vel illam volitionem eliciamus; & per consequens ex infallibilitate decretorum divinorum non sequi omnes actiones nostras liberas evenire necessario necessitate causali: quia tantum ex illa infallibilitate decretorum sequitur actiones nostras liberas evenire necessario ea necessitate consequentiae, quae non est causalis vel motiva. Atque adeo decreta Providentiae Dei non magis tollent libertatem arbitrii nostri, & contingentiam nostrarum actionum, quam praescientia Dei: sicut enim res non ideo eventura est, quia praescita est, ita etiam nos non ideo acturi sumus, secundum has vel illas actiones, quia Deus decrevit nobiscum concurrere ad has vel illas actiones eliciendas: sed potius Deus decrevit concurrere ad tales actiones, quia praevidit nos ita acturos.
english: From this, he goes on to say, it plainly follows that God by the decrees of his providence does not impose on us a necessity of willing this or that. Nor are God's decrees the causes why we produce this or that volition at this or that time.

So it does not follow from the infallibility of the divine decrees that all our free actions come about necessarily by a causal necessity. From that infallibility it follows only that our free actions come about necessarily by the necessity of consequence, which is neither causal nor motive.

Thus the decrees of God's providence will no more remove the freedom of our choice and the contingency of our actions than God's foreknowledge does. A thing will not come about because it is foreknown; likewise we shall not act in these or those ways because God decreed to concur with us in producing these or those actions. Rather, God decreed to concur in such actions because he foresaw that we would act so.

source_text: VII. Joannes Strangius Scotus vir ante paucos annos inter suos celeberrimus, hic singulari quadam ratione philosophatur. Nam aeterna Dei decreta circa omnes & singulos hominum actus versari concedit, sed non eodem modo. Primo enim quod attinet actus malos, ex ejus sententia, objiciuntur decretis divinis, non quod Deus illos fieri decreverit & praedefinierit, sed quia Deus decrevit permittere ut fiant, tum bonum ex illis elicere, eosque ad fines varios ordinare. Illam autem permissionem efficacem esse negat, id est, talem, ut ea posita, necessario sequatur quicquid fieri permittitur.
english: The Scot John Strang, a few years ago one of the most celebrated men of his own side, reasons here in a way of his own. He grants that God's eternal decrees concern each and every human act, but not all in the same way.

First, evil acts, in his view, are objects of the divine decrees not because God decreed and predefined that they should be done, but because God decreed to permit them to be done, then to bring good out of them and order them to various ends. He denies, however, that this permission is efficacious, that is, such that once it is in place whatever is permitted follows necessarily.

source_text: VIII. Quod spectat autem actus quibus natura sua malitia annexa non est, vult eos omnes dici posse a Deo decretos atque praedefinitos, sed rursus non omnes eadem ratione. Alios enim, juxta ipsum, Deus absolute decrevit, alios autem respective. Intelligit autem illa absolute a Deo decerni & praedefiniri, quae ante considerationem voluntatis nostrae decrevit, imo ad quae statuit voluntatem nostram praedeterminare. Respective vero, quae Deus decrevit fore secundum liberam nostram electionem, in iis in quibus liberam nobis optionem concedit, ita ut licitum sit hoc vel illud eligere.
english: As for acts that are not by their nature joined to malice, he holds that all of them can be said to be decreed and predefined by God, but again not all in the same way. Some, on his view, God decreed absolutely, others respectively.

By 'absolutely' decreed and predefined he means those that God decreed before considering our will, indeed those to which he resolved to predetermine our will. By 'respectively' he means those that God decreed would come about according to our free choice, in matters where he grants us a free option, so that we may lawfully choose this or that.

source_text: IX. Priori modo censet Deum decrevisse & praedefiniisse omnes actus vere bonos, & qui per se ad aeternam hominis salutem conferunt, ad quos Deus ab aeterno constituit voluntatem nostram efficaciter praedeterminare, ut revera illam in tempore actu praedeterminat. Sed praeter bona hominum opera, existimat quoque multa alia esse ex eorum genere quibus malitia necessario non adhaeret, ad quae voluntas hominum in tempore a Deo praedeterminatur, & consequenter quae fuerunt ab aeterno a Deo absolute decreta atque praedefinita, ut exempli gratia, heroica Cyri gesta, & quae erga Josephum Pharao Rex Aegypti gessit, & infinita ejusdem generis.
english: In the first way, he judges, God decreed and predefined all truly good acts, those that of themselves contribute to man's eternal salvation. To these God resolved from eternity to predetermine our will efficaciously, just as in time he actually does predetermine it.

Besides men's good works, he also thinks there are many other acts of a kind to which malice does not necessarily cling, to which God predetermines men's wills in time. These were therefore decreed and predefined by God absolutely from eternity: for example, the heroic deeds of Cyrus, what Pharaoh king of Egypt did for Joseph, and countless things of the same kind.

source_text: X. Veruntamen ut putat voluntatem hominum ad multos actus etiam ex se non malos, absolute a Deo in tempore non praedeterminari, sed liberam ipsi optionem permitti, ex duobus aut pluribus, quae utraque aut omnia sunt licita; sic etiam non putat omnes voluntatis actus, etiam qui peccati rationem non habent, fuisse absolute a Deo praedefinitos in aeternis ipsius decretis: sed, ut loquitur, respective solum; quia scilicet, praedefiniti non sunt ante & citra considerationem determinationis voluntatis creatae, sed cum respectu ad eam.
english: Even so, he thinks that for many acts which are not evil in themselves, men's wills are not absolutely predetermined by God in time; they are left a free option between two or more alternatives, all of them lawful.

Likewise he does not think that all acts of the will, even those without the character of sin, were absolutely predefined by God in his eternal decrees. They were predefined, in his phrase, only 'respectively': not before and apart from considering how the created will would determine itself, but with regard to that determination.

source_text: XI. Verbi causa, inquit, tria ista quae Deus permisit Optioni Davidis capite vigesimo quarto libri secundi Samuelis, omnia erant licita, id est, quodvis eorum potuit David licite eligere. Permissio enim horum Dei respectu non solum fuit Physica, sed etiam moralis. Deus permisit ei liberam optionem, ut quodcunque ex tribus mallet, id eligeret, non restrinxit ad unum, itaque non decrevit ut solum unum eligeret: sed praescius futurae electionis Davidis, ejusque habita ratione, recte dici potest simpliciter decrevisse pestem futuram, & septuaginta millia hominum occisum iri. Deus enim decrevit id efficere quod David electurus erat, hoc autem electurum eum Deus praeviderat; ergo hoc idem efficere Deus decrevit. De voluntate Dei circa peccatum lib. 3. cap. 2.
english: He offers an example, saying: the three things God left to David's choice in 2 Samuel 24 were all lawful options; David could rightly pick any of them, since God's leave here was moral and not merely physical.

God left him free to take whichever of the three he liked best, did not confine him to one, and so made no decree that he should choose only one. Yet because God knew in advance what David would choose and took that into account, one may rightly say that God simply decreed that pestilence should come and that seventy thousand men should be killed.

God decreed to carry out whatever David would choose; he had foreseen that David would choose this; so it was this that God decreed to carry out. (Strang, On the Will of God concerning Sin, book 3, chapter 2.)

source_text: XII. Ibidem vero rem illam illustrat simili quod occurrit inter homines. Si rex, inquit, servo suo optionem concedat hoc vel illud, vel tertium praemium aut munus eligendi ac petendi, certe non decrevit eum restringere ad unum horum; sed decrevit dare ei illud certum praemium, aut munus quod ille elegerit aut petierit. Multo magis id de Deo dici potest. Rex enim servo optionem dedit, ignarus forte ac incertus quid ille electurus esset. At Deo, quem nihil latere potest, ab aeterno certum erat quid David electurus esset.
english: In the same place he illustrates the point with a comparison from human life. 'If a king,' he says, 'gives his servant the option of choosing and asking for this reward or gift, or that one, or a third, he certainly has not decreed to restrict him to one of them. He has decreed to give him the particular reward or gift that the servant chooses or asks for.

This can be said of God much more. The king gave the servant the option perhaps without knowing, and uncertain, what he would choose. But to God, from whom nothing can be hidden, it was certain from eternity what David would choose.'

source_text: XIII. Sub finem vero capitis rem eandem accuratius explicat his verbis, Quotiescunque Deus permittit creatae voluntatis arbitrio electionem & optionem ad duo aut plura, vel ad agendum aut non agendum, non est existimandum Deum illam ad unam duntaxat partem restringere. Sed si decreto permissionis praescientiam Dei conjungamus de eventu futuro, sic dici potest Deum praedefinivisse singulos actus licitos qui eveniunt, quia ipse eam libertatem voluntati concedit, & cum ea cooperatur, idemque ab aeterno decrevit. Non quod Deus prius praeviderit eventum futurum, ac deinde eum decreverit fore; id enim ineptum esset, nempe illud decernere futurum, quod ante decretum praescivit esse futurum; nec quod Deus prius absolute decernat, ac deinde id praesciat futurum. Nam sic non permisisset, nec decrevisset permittere libero voluntatis arbitrio ut id & aliud ageret & non ageret: sed quod uno eodemque instanti simul praesciat ac decernat seu praedefiniat. Certe in aeternitate nihil est prius aut posterius; itaque cum praescientia & praedefinitio sint ab aeterno, neutra est altera prior aut posterior. Nos quidem pro nostro concipiendi modo, diversa rationis instantia distinguimus in aeternis Dei actibus. Sed nec secundum instantia rationis unam altera priorem aut posteriorem dicimus.
english: Toward the end of the chapter he explains the matter more precisely in these words. 'Whenever God leaves to the choice of the created will an election and option between two or more things, or between acting and not acting, we must not think that God restricts it to one side only.

But if we join to the decree of permission God's foreknowledge of the future event, it can be said that God predefined each lawful act that comes about. For he himself grants that freedom to the will, cooperates with it, and decreed the same from eternity.

This is not because God first foresaw the future event and then decreed that it would be; that would be absurd, to decree as future what he already foreknew to be future before the decree. Nor is it because God first decrees absolutely and then foreknows the thing as future. In that case he would not have permitted, or decreed to permit, the will's free choice to do and not do this and other things. It is because in one and the same instant he both foreknows and decrees, or predefines.

In eternity there is certainly nothing prior or posterior. Since foreknowledge and predefinition are both from eternity, neither comes before or after the other. In our way of conceiving we do distinguish different instants of reason in God's eternal acts. But even by instants of reason we do not call one of these prior or posterior to the other.'

source_text: XIV. Ut autem decreta divina cum voluntatis humanae libertate conciliet, duplicem voluntatis libertatem distinguit. Unam latius & communius sumptam, quae voluntati essentialis est, & in eo consistit quod voluntas proprio suo motu, certoque rationis judicio movetur: Alteram sensu strictiore acceptam, quam constituit in quadam voluntatis indifferentia ad opposita duo vel plura. Decreta Dei quibus absolute voluntatis actus praedefiniti sunt, fatetur hanc posteriorem libertatem tollere, quandoquidem voluntatem ad unum praedeterminant, nec sinunt amplius eam indifferentem ut agat vel non agat: sed ex ejus sententia voluntatem non privant libertate priori, quia haec optime consistunt, ut voluntas rationis judicium sequatur, & motu naturae suae consentaneo feratur, & tamen ad agendum a Deo praedefinita, & in tempore praedeterminata sit; quoniam scilicet, Deus voluntatem movet suaviter, & eo modo qui congruit & conveniens est naturae voluntatis.
english: To reconcile the divine decrees with the freedom of the human will, he distinguishes two kinds of freedom of the will. One, taken more broadly and commonly, is essential to the will: it consists in the will's being moved by its own motion and by a definite judgement of reason. The other, taken in a stricter sense, he locates in a kind of indifference of the will toward two or more opposites.

He admits that the decrees of God by which acts of the will are absolutely predefined remove this second freedom, since they predetermine the will to one thing and no longer leave it indifferent to act or not act.

But on his view they do not deprive the will of the first freedom. It fits perfectly well that the will should follow the judgement of reason and be carried by a motion in keeping with its nature, and yet be predefined by God to act and predetermined in time. For God moves the will gently, in a way that suits and befits the will's nature.

source_text: XV. Caeterum decreta Dei quibus mala fieri permittit, aut quosdam voluntatis actus non absolute sed tantum respective praedefinivit, voluntatem, juxta ipsum, liberam sinunt non solum priori & latiori sensu, sed etiam sensu illo posteriori atque strictiori, quia nempe antecedenter ad voluntatis ipsius determinationem, ab ea non auferunt indifferentiam ut agat vel non agat. Si quidem Dei permissio in eo statu voluntatem relinquit, ut possit quod permittitur agere vel non agere: quae vero sunt a Deo respective decreta, non, ut jam dictum est, praedefinita sunt ante & citra considerationem determinationis ipsius voluntatis, quae prolixius exposita videre est apud eundem Strangium lib. 2. c. 8.
english: The decrees of God by which he permits evils to be done, or by which he predefined certain acts of the will not absolutely but only respectively, leave the will free, on his view, not only in the first and broader sense but also in the second and stricter one. Prior to the will's own determination they do not take from it the indifference to act or not act.

God's permission leaves the will in a state where it can do or not do what is permitted. And what God decreed respectively was not, as already said, predefined before and apart from considering how the will itself would determine itself. This is set out at greater length in Strang, book 2, chapter 8.

source_text: XVI. Proinde secundum hujus viri doctrinam, quanquam homo in pluribus quae in hac vita degens agit, illa libertate gaudeat quae sita est in potestate ad opposita se determinandi; plurium tamen aliorum respectu quae sunt absolute Dei decreto praedefinita, libertatem eam non retinet, sed eam solum quae in eo sita est quod homo libens agit, & ex rationis propriae judicio. Quod praecipue locum habere putat in conversione hominis ad Deum & operibus gratiae. Nam, inquit, citra praedeterminationem Dei non potest homo converti, non potest pie agere; & posita praedeterminatione gratiae, non potest non converti, non potest non pie agere. Proinde in illis operibus etsi agnoscamus manere libertatem, quae voluntati est essentialis, tamen libertatem in strictiore isto sensu usurpatam illic locum habere negamus.
english: On this man's teaching, then, in most of what he does in this life man enjoys the freedom that consists in the power to determine himself to either of two opposites. But with respect to many other acts that are absolutely predefined by God's decree he does not keep that freedom, only the freedom that consists in acting willingly and by the judgement of his own reason.

He thinks this holds above all in man's conversion to God and in the works of grace. 'Without God's predetermination,' he says, 'a man cannot be converted and cannot act piously; and once the predetermination of grace is in place, he cannot fail to be converted and cannot fail to act piously. So although we acknowledge that the freedom essential to the will remains in those works, we deny that freedom in the stricter sense has any place there.'

source_text: XVII. Hic quoque viam singularem sequi videtur inclytae & celeberrimae memoriae vir Moses Amyraldus. Ille ergo quaecunque ab hominibus fiunt sive bona, sive mala, sive de eorum genere quae habentur indifferentia, aeternis Dei decretis designata, & praedefinita esse existimat, eaque decreta certissime & indeclinabiliter executioni mandari: sic tamen ut nec in eo violetur hominis libertas, nec Deus autor peccati statuatur.
english: Moses Amyraut, a man of renowned and most celebrated memory, also seems to follow a way of his own here. He holds that whatever men do, whether good, evil, or of the kind counted indifferent, is designated and predefined by God's eternal decrees.
Those decrees, he holds, are carried out with complete certainty and without fail, yet in such a way that human freedom is not violated and God is not made the author of sin.

source_text: XVIII. Ut autem modum explicet quo ista simul constant, supponit hominis facultates liberas, quales sunt juxta ipsum intellectus & voluntas, ab objectis determinari. Voluntatem enim necessario sequi dictamen intellectus, neque hominem posse aliter velle quam volendum esse judicat: Si vero intellectui sic vel sic affecto atque disposito, objectum hoc aut illud, sub tali luce proponatur, id est, his vel illis rationum momentis instructum & munitum, ita ut sit proportio & convenientia inter objectum tale & intellectum prout tunc se habet, necessario intellectum ad assensum vel dissensum determinandum esse, & hoc aut illud judicium de objecto sibi oblato determinate pronunciaturum, prout exiget ista proportio seu convenientia, quae inter intellectum & objectum fore supponitur.
english: To explain how these things fit together, he assumes that man's free faculties, which on his view are the intellect and the will, are determined by their objects. He holds that the will necessarily follows the dictate of the intellect, and that a man cannot will otherwise than he judges ought to be willed.

Suppose an intellect affected and disposed in this or that way, and suppose this or that object is put before it in a certain light, that is, equipped and backed by these or those weighty reasons, so that there is a proportion and fit between such an object and the intellect as it then stands. Then the intellect must necessarily be determined to assent or dissent.
It must then pronounce this or that definite judgement about the object offered to it, as required by the proportion or fit assumed to hold between the intellect and the object.

source_text: XIX. Nec istam necessitatem seu determinationem, quae juxta ipsum oritur a convenientia objecti cum facultate, libertati quicquam officere putat, quoniam libertatem non constituit in facultatis liberae indeterminatione & indifferentia & immunitate ab omni necessitate, sed cum ea pugnare putat eam solum necessitatem quae est a vi externa, a materia, vel a sensu, quam Physicam & brutam appellare possumus, aut saltem eam quae tollit omnem consultationem & deliberationem.
english: Nor does he think that this necessity or determination, which on his view arises from the fit between object and faculty, hinders freedom at all, since he does not place freedom in the free faculty's indetermination, indifference and immunity from all necessity.

He thinks freedom conflicts only with the necessity that comes from external force, from matter or from sense, which we may call physical and brute necessity, or at least with the necessity that removes all consultation and deliberation.

source_text: XX. Deinde Providentiae Divinae efficaciam qua divina decreta executioni mandantur, respectu humanarum actionum in genere, in eo constituit quod Deus hominis facultates conservat, & objecta varia modis variis atque innumeris illis offerri vel auferri vel sinit vel procurat; Unde necessario & infallibiliter oriuntur actiones decretis Dei designatae, & tamen liberarum facultatum naturae ac dispositioni, & objectorum ipsis propositorum conditioni congruentes, ac proinde liberae: quandoquidem vis nulla facultatibus illata est, nec earum libertatem ullo modo violat objectorum quorumcunque oblatio & propositio.
english: Next, with respect to human actions in general, he locates the efficacy of God's providence, by which the divine decrees are carried out, in this: God preserves man's faculties and, in various and countless ways, either allows or arranges that various objects be offered to them or withdrawn.

From this the actions designated by God's decrees arise necessarily and infallibly. Yet they suit the nature and disposition of the free faculties and the condition of the objects put before them, and so they are free. No force is brought to bear on the faculties, and the offering and presenting of objects of any kind in no way violates their freedom.

source_text: XXI. Speciatim vero respectu bonarum actionum, praeterea quae jam dicta sunt, non aliud Deo tribuit quam quod facultates ipsas ab adnatis vitiis repurgat, aut novis viribus instruit, & supra nativam ac primigeniam conditionem elevat, quibus actionibus libertatem earum nihil omnino laedi sed adjuvari potius planum est.
english: With respect to good actions in particular, beyond what has already been said, he ascribes to God only this: that he cleanses the faculties themselves of their inborn faults, or supplies them with new strength and raises them above their native, original condition.
Plainly such acts do not harm the faculties' freedom at all, but rather help it.

source_text: XXII. Quod spectat autem malas actiones quantumcunque decretis divinis subjaceant, ex suis principiis ostendi facile posse existimat Deum nullatenus earum authorem dici posse: quoniam Deus hominum mentem & voluntatem ad malum non inclinat, nec eas ulla ratione vitiat, sed solum proprios motus ultro exerere sinit: neque alia ratione circa eas versatur divina providentia, quam quod ista potius quam alia objecta, hacque potius quam illa ratione ipsis offerri procurat aut permittit. Unde tamen necessario resultant istae vel illae actiones, prout exigit relatio proportionis & convenientiae inter talia objecta, & facultates sic vel sic affectas. Quo fit ut decreta divina de illis & circa illas indeclinabiliter executioni mandentur: nec minus interea facultates ipsae libere moveantur; quandoquidem vis nulla ipsis infertur, neque aliter agunt quam fert ipsarum natura atque dispositio.
english: As for evil actions, however fully they are subject to the divine decrees, he thinks it can easily be shown from his principles that God can in no way be called their author. God does not incline men's minds and wills to evil or corrupt them in any way; he only allows them to put forth their own motions of their own accord.

Divine providence is involved with these actions only in arranging or permitting that these objects rather than others be offered to them, and in this way rather than that. From this, nevertheless, these or those actions necessarily result, as the relation of proportion and fit between such objects and faculties disposed in this or that way requires.

So the divine decrees about them are carried out without fail, and meanwhile the faculties themselves move freely, since no force is applied to them and they act only as their own nature and disposition lead.

source_text: XXIII. Cum ergo Deus circa hominum facultates, seu in bonum seu in malum ferantur, nihil operetur quod cum earum nativa libertate repugnet, & tamen ad Dei operationem infallibiliter sequantur isti vel illi actus sive boni sive mali; Deus autem non aliter res ab aeterno decreverit quam exequitur in tempore: inde colligit haec optime consistere, ut homines libere agant, & interim dum libere agunt ea peragant inevitabiliter quae aeternis Dei decretis constituta & designata sunt. Quae latius diducta videre licet apud virum illum Doctissimum disputatione de libero arbitrio capite quarto.
english: God, then, does nothing to men's faculties, whether they are carried toward good or toward evil, that conflicts with their native freedom. Yet upon God's working these or those acts, good or evil, follow infallibly, and God decreed things from eternity exactly as he carries them out in time.

From this Amyraut concludes that it fits perfectly well that men act freely and that, while acting freely, they inevitably accomplish what God's eternal decrees have appointed and designated. This is worked out more fully by that most learned man in his disputation on free choice, chapter 4.

source_text: XXIV. Caeterum ad difficultatem istam expediendam viam paulo diversam insistunt Scholae Reformatae Theologi complures. Non solum enim docent quaecunque ab hominibus fiunt aeternis Dei decretis esse praedefinita, sed decreta illa putant effectum suum sortiri, non solum, ut censet vir ille Doctissimus, per aliquam facultatum liberarum immutationem, quae in earum restitutione, aut novarum virium adjectione consistat, ac praeterea per variorum objectorum tum intus tum extra propositionem, verum etiam per physicam & realem efficaciam, qua facultates ipsae ad hos & illos actus liberos praemoveantur, & praedeterminentur.
english: To deal with this difficulty, however, a good number of theologians of the Reformed school take a somewhat different path. They teach not only that whatever men do is predefined by God's eternal decrees, but also that those decrees take effect by more than that most learned man holds.

They do not work only through some change in the free faculties, consisting in their restoration or the addition of new strength, together with the presenting of various objects from within and from without. They also work through a physical and real efficacy by which the faculties themselves are premoved and predetermined to these and those free acts.

source_text: XXV. Nempe haec est eorum doctrina, Absoluto & energetico ut loquuntur Dei decreto quaecunque fiunt a causis etiam liberis & contingentibus decreta & ordinata esse. Hoc decretum nunquam irritum esse posse, sed omnino necesse esse ut impleantur quae sic a Deo decreta sunt. Adeoque illa ipsa quae causae contingentes & liberae operantur, hujus decreti respectu necessario fieri nec aliter evenire posse.
english: Their teaching is this. By an absolute and, as they call it, 'energetic' decree of God, whatever is done even by free and contingent causes has been decreed and ordered. This decree can never fail, and what God has so decreed must without exception be fulfilled.
So the very things that contingent and free causes do are done necessarily with respect to this decree, and cannot turn out otherwise.
